Chapter 2: Choosing Optimism—Finding Light in Difficult Times.
You know, optimism doesn’t just show up on its own. It’s a choice—one we have to make again and again, especially when life seems determined to make things tough. If you’re facing a chronic illness, optimism can feel so delicate—easy to lose, and sometimes nearly impossible to hold onto. But it’s more than just a feeling. It’s a tool we can use, something that helps us shape our experience and find meaning, even in the middle of hardship.
After getting that diagnosis, optimism felt unnatural at first. There were mornings when even getting out of bed seemed impossible, when the future felt heavy and overwhelming. But then, there were brief moments—a friend’s kind word, the sound of a child laughing, a peaceful afternoon with family—that offered tiny glimpses of something brighter. These moments didn’t make the pain disappear, but they made it manageable.
Work changed, too. What once gave me pride and a sense of identity suddenly became complicated. On set, every move felt watched, every line had to be delivered perfectly. There was a constant fear of being found out, of letting others see just how tough things really were. But slowly, the urge to hide faded. Colleagues I’d kept at a distance started to become friends. Some of them shared their own struggles, and suddenly, the workplace turned into a community—imperfect people doing their best, together.
I learned optimism isn’t about pretending everything’s fine. It’s about seeing the whole picture—the pain and the possibility, the loss and the love. It means being honest about the hard days, but also celebrating the good ones. It’s finding humor in places you’d never expect, and not letting fear have the last word.
Of course, there were setbacks. Sometimes treatments didn’t work. Symptoms got worse. Plans had to change. But each new challenge brought its own lessons. Patience, which I’d never had much of before, became essential. Flexibility wasn’t just helpful—it was a way of life. And even though the future felt uncertain, there was hope in that uncertainty. After all, anything could happen—including good things.
Family made all the difference. Kids, with their energy and curiosity, reminded me every day what really matters. My partner’s steady support gave me a foundation of trust and love. Together, we built little rituals—sharing meals, reading bedtime stories, taking quiet walks—that kept us grounded, even when the future felt scary.
Faith played its part, too. Not necessarily in a religious way, but in believing that life is still worth living, even when it’s hard. That meaning can be found in the smallest moments. That hope, once you choose it, can actually grow.
So, optimism didn’t erase the challenges of living with Parkinson’s. But it did change how I faced them. It turned obstacles into chances to grow. Setbacks became opportunities to learn. And it made it possible to look up, even when it felt like the world wanted me to keep looking down.
